On such evenings, poor Mr. Woodhouse was in great internal conflict. A small bowl of thin gruel like his own was all he could recommend with complete satisfaction; though he might manage, while the ladies were comfortably finishing the more delicate dishes, to say:

“Mrs. Bates, let me suggest you try one of these eggs. An egg boiled very softly is not unhealthy. Serle understands boiling eggs better than anyone. I would not recommend an egg boiled by anyone else; but you need not worry, they are very small, you see—one of our small eggs will not harm you. Miss Bates, let Emma assist you with a little piece of tart—a very little piece. Ours are all apple tarts. You need not fear unhealthy preserves here. I do not advise the custard. Emma allowed her father to speak—but she provided her guests in a much more satisfying manner, and on the present evening had particular pleasure in sending them away happy. I saw all this in an instant, for I had only a moment to take it in: he cursed at me, swung at me—it was a feeble round blow that missed me and nearly knocked himself over, for it made him stumble—and then he ran into the fog, stumbling twice as he went, and I lost sight of him.

'It’s the young man!' I thought, my heart leaping as I recognized him. I suppose I would have felt a pain in my liver too, if I had known where it was.

I soon reached the Battery after that, and there was the correct man—hugging himself and limping back and forth, as if he had never stopped hugging and limping all night—waiting for me. His eyes looked so dreadfully hungry too, that when I gave him the file and he placed it on the grass, it occurred to me he might have tried to eat it, if he had not noticed my bundle. 'Brandy,' I replied.

'I think you have the ague,' I said.

'I agree with you, boy,' he said.

When evaluating an author's worth and determining their place among the literary pantheon, we are justified in assessing them from our own perspective and according to our own criteria. Yet, when considering the strength of their work, we must take into account their original intent and compare their creations to the vision they themselves set forth, measuring how much falls short. We differ from Mr. Poe in our views on the aims of art. He believes the goal is the creation of Beauty, and it may be only in the interpretation of that term that we find ourselves at odds. In our remarks on his writings, however, we shall follow his own standard as our guide. The sanctuary of the muse is open from every direction, and there is ample space within it for all who offer tribute or seek prophecy.

In his stories, Mr. Poe has chosen to demonstrate his talent primarily in that shadowy realm that lies at the edge of the plausible and stretches into the strange boundaries of superstition and the unreal. He possesses a striking ability to blend two faculties rarely found together: the capacity to affect the reader's mind with the subtle suggestions of mystery and an attention to detail so thorough that not even a pin or a button escapes notice. Both traits stem naturally from the dominant feature of his intellect, which we have previously mentioned—analysis. This is what sets the artist apart. His mind immediately grasps the desired effect. Once he has decided to evoke certain feelings in the reader, he ensures that every element contributes precisely to the central aim. Even his mystery is calculated in his mind. To him, X is a known variable throughout. In any scene he creates, he understands the chemical nature of all his colors. Although some of his figures may appear indistinct, and the shadows formless, to him the contours are as clear and defined as those of a geometric figure. For this reason, Mr. Poe has no affinity for Mysticism. The Mystic lives within the mystery, is wrapped in it; it tinges all his thoughts; it especially affects his vision, and the most ordinary things acquire a prismatic glow from it. Mr. Poe, by contrast, is an observer from the outside. He examines, he dissects, he watches

“with an eye serene,
The very pulse of the machine,”

for it is essentially a machine to him, with gears and cogs and piston-rods, all working to achieve a specific outcome.

This analytical nature of his mind tempers the poetic, and by giving him the endurance to be meticulous, allows him to inject a remarkable sense of reality into his most fantastical ideas. A monomania he portrays with great strength. He enjoys dissecting one of these mental tumors and tracing all the delicate extensions of its roots. In conjuring images of horror, too, he achieves unusual success, sometimes conveying to us by a faint suggestion some dreadful uncertainty, which is the essence of all horror. He leaves the imagination the task of completing the picture, a task to which only it is suited.

“For much imaginary work was there;
Conceit deceitful, so compact, so kind,
That for Achilles’ image stood his spear
Grasped in an armed hand; himself behind
Was left unseen, save to the eye of mind.”

Our first knowledge of Mr. Poe's relocation to this city came through a visit we received from a lady who introduced herself to us as the mother of his wife. It was a difficult fate she was watching over. Mr. Poe wrote with great difficulty and in a style too elevated for the general public to appreciate, and thus he was poorly compensated.

I also brought along a pair of pigeons and a cat. It was now almost dawn, and I felt it was time to leave. Pretending to drop a lit cigar, I used the moment to crouch and quietly set fire to the slow match, the end of which slightly extended beyond the rim of one of the smaller barrels. The three men who had been pestering me noticed nothing of this. I jumped into the car and severed the single rope tethering me to the ground, delighted to see that I rose easily, carrying one hundred and seventy-five pounds of lead ballast, with the capacity to lift as much more.

“Yet scarcely had I reached fifty yards in height when a terrible storm of fire, smoke, sulfur, limbs, gravel, burning wood, and glowing metal surged upward after me in a most dreadful and chaotic fashion. My heart sank, and I fell to the bottom of the car, shaking with sheer terror. At that moment, I realized I had overestimated the situation, and the full impact of the blast was yet to come. Almost immediately, I felt a rush of blood to my temples, followed by a jarring shock that I shall never forget, which tore through the night and seemed to split the very heavens. Later, I was able to understand that the intensity of the explosion on me was due to my position directly above it, in the path of its greatest force. But at the time, I was only concerned with saving my life. The balloon first collapsed, then violently expanded, then spun wildly at a terrifying speed, and finally, swaying and lurching like a drunkard, it hurled me over the edge of the car with great force, leaving me hanging at a terrifying height, head down and face outward, by a slender cord about three feet long, which had accidentally caught through a crack in the wicker and entangled my left foot as I fell. I gasped for breath convulsively, a shudder like a fit of the ague shook every nerve and muscle in my body, my eyes seemed to pop from their sockets, a terrible nausea overwhelmed me—and finally, I lost consciousness.

What melody the Syrens sang, or what name Achilles took when he disguised himself among women, though they are puzzling, are not entirely beyond guesswork.

The mental traits described as analytical are, in themselves, not easily broken down. We understand them only through their effects. We know that for those who possess them in excess, they bring the greatest joy. Just as a strong man takes pride in his physical strength, enjoying tasks that test his muscles, so the analyst takes pride in the mental act of unraveling. He finds pleasure even in the smallest tasks that engage his abilities. He enjoys riddles, wordplay, and symbols; in solving them, he shows a level of sharpness that seems almost supernatural to most. His conclusions, achieved through the very core of method, truly resemble intuition.

The ability to break things down may be greatly strengthened by studying mathematics, especially its highest branch, which, unfairly and due to its backward process, has been labeled, as if by right, analysis. Yet calculation alone is not analysis. A chess player, for example, performs the former without effort toward the latter. It follows that the game of chess, in its impact on the mind, is often misunderstood. I am not composing a formal essay now, but merely introducing a somewhat unusual story with some random observations; I will therefore take the chance to claim that the higher functions of the reflective mind are more clearly and usefully tested by the modest game of checkers than by all the elaborate frivolity of chess. In chess, where the pieces move in different and strange ways, with varying and shifting values, what is merely complex is often mistaken (a common mistake) for what is deep. Here, attention is strongly engaged. If it wavers for a moment, a mistake is made, leading to loss or failure. The possible moves being not only numerous but intricate, the chances of such errors increase; and in nine out of ten cases, it is the more focused rather than the more clever player who wins. In checkers, on the other hand, where the moves are fixed and have little variation, the chances of error are reduced, and the mere attention is left relatively free, so that any advantage gained by either side comes from greater insight. To be more concrete, let us imagine a game of checkers where the pieces are limited to four kings, and where, of course, no mistake is expected. It is clear that here the outcome (with both players being equally skilled) can only be decided by some clever move, the result of a strong effort of the mind. Stripped of usual tools, the analyst enters the mindset of his opponent, aligns himself with it, and often sees, at a glance, the only methods (sometimes absurdly simple) by which he might lead the opponent into error or rush into a miscalculation.

"We should not assess the methods," Dupin remarked, "based on this cursory examination. The Parisian police, often praised for their sharpness, are clever, but that is all. The scent had never for a moment been lost. Not a single link in the chain showed any flaw. I had followed the mystery to its final outcome—and that outcome was the nail. It appeared exactly like its counterpart in the other window, yet this similarity was of no consequence (though it might seem otherwise) when compared to the fact that the trail ended here. The break was old (its edges were covered in rust), and it was clearly the result of a hammer blow, which had driven the head of the nail partially into the top of the bottom sash. I now carefully returned this head to the indentation from which I had removed it, and the resemblance to a complete nail was perfect—the crack was invisible. Pressing the spring, I gently raised the sash a few inches; the head moved up with it, remaining firmly in place. I closed the window, and the appearance of the entire nail was once again flawless. To me, this piece seems to prove little beyond the enthusiasm of its author. We must remember that, generally speaking, newspapers aim more to provoke a reaction—to make a point—than to advance the cause of truth. The latter is only pursued when it aligns with the former. A publication that merely agrees with common opinion (however sound this opinion may be) gains no favor with the public. The majority of people consider profound only those who offer sharp contradictions to the prevailing thought. In reasoning, no less than in writing, it is the witty remark that is most quickly and widely appreciated. In both, it is the least commendable form of expression. 'What I mean to say is, that it is the blend of wit and drama in the idea—that Marie Rogêt is still alive—that has led L’Etoile to propose this theory, rather than any genuine likelihood of the idea. Let us consider the points of this journal’s argument, striving to avoid the confusion with which it is originally presented. 'The first goal of the writer is to demonstrate, based on the short time between Marie’s disappearance and the discovery of the floating body, that this body cannot be Marie’s. Reducing this time to its shortest possible length thus becomes the immediate aim of the thinker. In his hasty pursuit of this aim, he jumps to an assumption right away. 'It is foolish to believe,' he states, 'that the murder, if it occurred on her body, could have been completed quickly enough to allow her killers to cast the body into the river before midnight.' We instantly and naturally ask, why? Why is it foolish to believe the murder took place just five minutes after the girl left her mother’s home? Why is it foolish to believe it occurred at any given time of the day? There have been murders at all hours. This assumption, then, amounts precisely to this—that the murder did not occur on Sunday at all—and, if we allow L’Etoile to make this assumption, we might as well allow it any liberties. Before daylight in the mornings I would sneak into cornfields and take a watermelon, or a mushmelon, or a punkin, or some fresh corn, or things like that. Pap always said it wasn’t any harm to borrow things if you meant to pay them back later; but the widow said it was just a soft name for stealing, and no decent person would do it. Jim said he thought the widow was partly right and pap was partly right; so the best way would be for us to pick out two or three things from the list and say we wouldn’t borrow them anymore—then he thought it wouldn’t be any harm to borrow the others. The best place to find canoes is near rafts that are tied up along the shore. But we didn't see any rafts tied up, so we floated along for more than three hours. The night turned gray and thick, almost like fog. You can't see the river's shape or anything far away in weather like that. It got very late and quiet, and then a steamboat came up the river. We lit the lantern, hoping it would catch their attention. Boats going upstream usually stay far away from us; they follow the sandbars and look for smooth water near the rocks. But on nights like this, they push right up the middle of the river.

We could hear the boat rumbling along, but we couldn't see it clearly until it was almost on top of us. It was heading straight for us. They often do that, trying to see how close they can get without hitting anything. Sometimes the wheel cuts off a piece of the raft, and then the pilot sticks his head out and laughs, thinking he's clever. Well, here it came, and we thought it was going to try to pass us closely; but it didn't seem to be turning away at all. It was a big boat, and it was moving fast, too, looking like a black cloud with rows of glow-worms around it. Then suddenly it expanded, big and frightening, with a long line of open furnace doors glowing like red-hot teeth, and its huge bow and guards hanging right over us. There was a shout at us, and the sound of bells to stop the engines, a lot of swearing, and steam hissing—and as Jim jumped into the water on one side and I on the other, it smashed straight through the raft.

I dove—and I meant to reach the bottom, too, because a thirty-foot wheel was going to pass over me, and I wanted it to have plenty of space. I could usually stay underwater for a minute; this time I guess I stayed under for a minute and a half. Then I shot up to the surface quickly, because I was about to burst. I came up to my armpits and blew the water out of my nose, and caught my breath. Of course there was a strong current; and of course the boat started its engines again ten seconds after it stopped them, because they didn't care much for raftsmen; so now it was churning up the river, out of sight in the thick weather, though I could still hear it.

I called out for Jim about a dozen times, but I didn't get any answer; so I grabbed a plank that brushed against me while I was treading water, and swam for the shore, pushing the plank ahead of me. But I noticed that the current was pulling me toward the left-hand shore, which meant I was in a crossing; so I changed direction and swam that way.

So we pushed off on the raft after dark.

I dove—and I was determined to find the bottom, too, because a thirty-foot wheel was going to pass over me, and I wanted to give it plenty of room. There was one where a young lady was at a window gazing up at the moon, with tears sliding down her cheeks; she held an open letter in one hand, showing black sealing wax on one edge, and pressed a locket with a chain against her mouth. Underneath the picture it read, 'And Art Thou Gone Yes Thou Art Gone Alas.' These were all nice pictures, I suppose, but somehow they didn't sit well with me, because they always made me feel worse when I was already feeling down. Everyone was sorry she passed away, because she had planned to do many more of these pictures, and you could tell by the ones she had completed what she had lost. But I figured, given her nature, she was probably having a better time in the graveyard. She was working on what they said was her greatest picture when she fell ill, and every day and night she prayed to be allowed to live until she finished it, but she never got the chance. It was a picture of a young woman in a long white dress, standing on the rail of a bridge, ready to jump, with her hair flowing down her back, looking up at the moon, tears streaming down her face, with two arms folded across her chest, two arms stretched out in front, and two more reaching up toward the moon—and the idea was to see which pair looked best, then scratch out the others; but, as I was saying, she died before she could decide, and now they kept this picture over the head of the bed in her room, and every time her birthday came around, they hung flowers on it. Other times it was covered with a small curtain. The young woman in the picture had a kind of sweet, gentle face, but with so many arms, she seemed too spidery to me.

This young girl kept a scrapbook while she was alive, and used to paste obituaries, accidents, and cases of patient suffering from the _Presbyterian Observer_ into it, and then write poetry of her own after them. It was very good poetry. This is what she wrote about a boy named Stephen Dowling Bots who fell down a well and drowned:

ODE TO STEPHEN DOWLING BOTS, DEC’D

And did young Stephen sicken,
And did young Stephen die?
And did the sad hearts thicken,
And did the mourners cry?

No; such was not the fate of
Young Stephen Dowling Bots;
Though sad hearts round him thickened,
’Twas not from sickness’ shots.

No whooping-cough did rack his frame,
Nor measles drear with spots;
Not these impaired the sacred name
Of Stephen Dowling Bots.

Despised love struck not with woe
That head of curly knots,
Nor stomach troubles laid him low,
Young Stephen Dowling Bots.

O no. Then list with tearful eye,
Whilst I his fate do tell.
His soul did from this cold world fly
By falling down a well.

They got him out and emptied him;
Alas it was too late;
His spirit was gone for to sport aloft
In the realms of the good and great.

The next Sunday we all went to church, about three miles away, everyone riding horseback. The men brought their guns along, Buck did too, and they kept them between their knees or propped them against the wall. The Shepherdsons did the same. The preaching was pretty dull—it was all about brotherly love and other tiring topics; but everyone said it was a fine sermon, and they talked about it on the way home, having so much to say about faith and good works and free grace and predestination, and all sorts of other things, that it seemed to me to be one of the toughest Sundays I had ever come across.

About an hour after dinner, everyone was lounging around, some in their chairs and some in their rooms, and it got pretty boring. Buck and a dog were lying on the grass in the sun, fast asleep. I went up to our room and thought I’d take a nap myself. I found sweet Miss Sophia standing in her doorway, which was next to ours, and she led me into her room and closed the door gently, asking me if I liked her, and I said I did; and she asked me if I would do something for her and not tell anyone, and I said I would. Then she said she had forgotten her Testament and left it in the church pew between two other books, and would I sneak out quietly and go get it for her and not say a word to anyone. I said I would. So I slipped out and hurried up the road, and there wasn’t a soul at the church, except maybe a couple of hogs, for the door wasn’t locked, and hogs like a puncheon floor in summer because it’s cool. If you notice, most folks don’t go to church unless they have to; but a hog is different.

I told myself something was up; it wasn’t natural for a girl to be so worked up about a Testament. So I shook it, and out fell a little scrap of paper with “Half-past two” written on it with a pencil. I went through it, but couldn’t find anything else. I couldn’t make heads or tails of it, so I put the paper back in the book, and when I got home and upstairs, there was Miss Sophia in her doorway waiting for me. She pulled me in and shut the door; then she looked through the Testament till she found the paper, and as soon as she read it she looked happy; and before you could think she hugged me and said I was the best boy in the world and not to tell anyone. She was quite red in the face for a minute, and her eyes lit up, and it made her very pretty. I was quite surprised, but when I caught my breath I asked her what the paper was about, and she asked me if I had read it, and I said no, and she asked me if I could read writing, and I told her “no, only big letters,” and then she said the paper wasn’t anything but a book-mark to keep her place, and I might go and play now.

As soon as it was dark we pushed off; when we got her out to about the middle we let her go, and let her float wherever the current wanted her to; then we lit the pipes, and dangled our legs in the water, and talked about all sorts of things—we were always naked, day and night, whenever the mosquitoes would let us—the new clothes Buck’s folks made for me was too good to be comfortable, and besides I didn’t go much on clothes, nohow.

Sometimes we’d have that whole river all to ourselves for the longest time. Yonder was the banks and the islands, across the water; and maybe a spark—which was a candle in a cabin window; and sometimes on the water you could see a spark or two—on a raft or a scow, you know; and maybe you could hear a fiddle or a song coming over from one of them crafts. It’s lovely to live on a raft. We had the sky up there, all speckled with stars, and we used to lay on our backs and look up at them, and discuss about whether they was made or only just happened. Jim he allowed they was made, but I allowed they happened; I judged it would have took too long to make so many. Jim said the moon could a laid them; well, that looked kind of reasonable, so I didn’t say nothing against it, because I’ve seen a frog lay most as many, so of course it could be done. We used to watch the stars that fell, too, and see them streak down. Jim allowed they’d got spoiled and was hove out of the nest.

Once or twice of a night we would see a steamboat slipping along in the dark, and now and then she would belch a whole world of sparks up out of her chimbleys, and they would rain down in the river and look awful pretty; then she would turn a corner and her lights would wink out and her powwow shut off and leave the river still again; and by-and-by her waves would get to us, a long time after she was gone, and joggle the raft a bit, and after that you wouldn’t hear nothing for you couldn’t tell how long, except maybe frogs or something.

The king pulled out an old, tattered deck of cards after breakfast, and he and the duke played seven-up for a while, five cents a game. Then they grew tired of it and decided they would 'lay out a campaign,' as they put it. The duke went into his carpet-bag and brought out a bunch of little printed notices and read them aloud. One notice said, 'The celebrated Dr. Armand de Montalban, of Paris,' would 'lecture on the Science of Phrenology' at a certain place, on the blank day of blank, for ten cents admission, and 'furnish charts of character at twenty-five cents apiece.' The duke said that was _him_. In another notice he was the 'world-renowned Shakespearian tragedian, Garrick the Younger, of Drury Lane, London.' In other notices he had a lot of other names and performed other amazing feats, like finding water and gold with a 'divining-rod,' 'dissipating witch spells,' and so on. After a while he said:

'But the histrionic muse is the darling. Have you ever trod the boards, Royalty?'

'No,' says the king.

'You shall, then, before you’re three days older, Fallen Grandeur,' says the duke. 'The first decent town we come to we’ll hire a hall and do the sword fight in Richard III. and the balcony scene in Romeo and Juliet. How does that strike you?'

'I’m in, up to the hub, for anything that will pay, Bilgewater; but, you see, I don’t know nothing about play-actin’, and hain’t ever seen much of it. I was too small when pap used to have ’em at the palace. Do you reckon you can learn me?'

'Easy!'

'All right. I’m just a-freezin’ for something fresh, anyway. Let’s commence right away.'

So the duke told him all about who Romeo was and who Juliet was, and said he was used to being Romeo, so the king could be Juliet.

'But if Juliet’s such a young gal, duke, my peeled head and my white whiskers is goin’ to look uncommon odd on her, maybe.'

'No, don’t you worry; these country jakes won’t ever think of that. Besides, you know, you’ll be in costume, and that makes all the difference in the world; Juliet’s in a balcony, enjoying the moonlight before she goes to bed, and she’s got on her night-gown and her ruffled nightcap. And he kept on walking around, talking to himself and enjoying the sound of his own voice, and every now and then he brought up the funeral ceremonies again, until the duke couldn’t take it anymore. He was the _worst_ I ever met. Well, the iron-jawed man laughed right in his face. Everyone was shocked. Everyone said, “Why, _doctor!_” and Abner Shackleford said:

The king smiled eagerly, held out his hand, and said:

“Keep your hands off of me!” said the doctor. “_You_ talk like an Englishman, _don’t_ you? It’s the worst imitation I ever heard. _You_ Peter Wilks’s brother! You’re a fraud, that’s what you are!”
